analysis.one_liner: Cut off the consumer watchdog's independent Fed funding and subject it to yearly congressional appropriations.
analysis.headline: A single House Republican introduced the bill with no cosponsors, and it never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the funding rules for the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the watchdog created after the 2008 financial crisis to police mortgages, credit cards, payday loans, and debt collection. Instead of receiving its money automatically from the Federal Reserve, the Bureau would have to ask Congress for money every year [S2]. The bill also repealed the Bureau's dedicated fund and authorized money only through fiscal year 2012, meaning Congress could simply decline to fund it [S2]. The bill died in committee without a single cosponsor or vote [S4][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: The financial firms the CFPB regulates — banks, mortgage lenders, payday lenders, debt collectors, and credit reporting companies — would benefit if the Bureau's funding could be blocked or cut during annual appropriations fights, since a smaller or stalled Bureau brings fewer investigations, fewer rules, and weaker enforcement against their practices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Banks and consumer-lending firms regulated by the CFPB

how_it_helps.text: Subjects the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to the regular authorization, budget, and appropriations process of the Treasury Department, instead of its automatic transfer from the Federal Reserve [S2][S3].
Repeals the annual transfer of Federal Reserve funds to the Bureau and repeals the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection Fund [S2][S3].
Replaces the FY2010–FY2014 authorization of appropriations with an authorization for only FY2012, after which the Bureau would have no guaranteed funding at all [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers. The CFPB's enforcement against predatory mortgages, unfair credit card fees, payday lending, and debt collection abuses would depend on Congress approving its budget each year, giving financial industry lobbying an annual choke point on the watchdog's work.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers facing predatory lending and fees

drawbacks.text: Supporters' honest best argument: the CFPB's independent funding is unusual among federal agencies, and routing it through the appropriations process is how Congress normally holds agencies accountable — a defensible accountability principle stated in the bill's own title and purpose [S2][S3].

The bill authorized funding for only fiscal year 2012 with nothing afterward, so even a supporter who wanted appropriations oversight rather than abolition was handed a mechanism that could simply shut the Bureau down [S2][S3].
Under the bill, the Bureau's budget would become an annual political bargaining chip, and any single chamber could withhold funds to stall enforcement investigations it disliked.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real argument for congressional oversight of agency budgets, but the bill's design undercut it: it authorized the Bureau's funding for a single year and repealed the fund that gave the watchdog stable money, which points toward defunding rather than accountability. The cost would fall on consumers, whose protection against predatory lending and fee abuses would hinge on yearly budget fights. The bill's own fate — zero cosponsors and no committee action — suggests even its would-be allies did not move it forward.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Financial Services Committee and then a subcommittee, and sat there with no markup, no vote, and no floor action until the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Posey (R-FL) introduced the bill in the House on April 15, 2011 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on April 15, 2011, and to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit on May 2, 2011 [S5].

The complete action history shows no committee markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, and no further action after the subcommittee referral for the remainder of the 112th Congress, which ended January 3, 2013 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau kept the independent funding structure created by the 2010 Dodd-Frank law, and consumers kept a watchdog whose budget financial firms and their congressional allies could not block year to year.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The consumer watchdog's independent funding survived

for.name: Rep. Bill Posey
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made no visible progress on it; it attracted no cosponsors [S4][S5].

against.name: Rep. Spencer Bachus
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never brought it to a committee markup or vote, leaving it to die in committee [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; a single House Republican introduced the bill, no one from either party cosponsored it, and it never advanced [S4][S5].

industries.note: These firms are CFPB-regulated; the bill would let Congress block or cut the watchdog's budget each year, weakening enforcement against their lending practices. The industry's gain is weaker oversight that ordinary consumers pay for in fees and abusive terms.

industries.industry: Payday lenders, debt collectors, and credit reporting companies
industries.note: These firms face some of the CFPB's most active enforcement; making the Bureau's funding dependent on annual congressional approval would give their allies a recurring opportunity to stall investigations.

The bill repealed the Bureau's dedicated fund and its Federal Reserve transfer, authorizing money for only one fiscal year — a funding cliff that would leave the agency unable to plan or, if appropriations failed, to operate.
